The fact of the matter is, is that the City of Lakewood, as well as all cities and municipalities, we're going to need some assistance from the federal government. You know, thus far, the federal government has been very good in addressing, you know, unemployment and assistance for just individual citizens. And of course, you know, huge, huge financial package is for business assistance. There has been some money that has come down through the CARES Act to local governments. However, there's two issues with that. The first is, is that the threshold of population in terms of who gets the money is 500,000 people. So that means in Washington state, the state of Washington received 1.6 billion dollars. Pierce County received 158 million. And then the only city that has received money directly is Seattle. The second challenge with the use of those monies is while they can be used for essential governmental services, they cannot be used for expenditures that have either already been adopted and budgeted for, or more importantly, to backfill any lost revenue. That is a congressional decision that came from Congress and is flowing through the Treasury Department. On a number of fronts, we are working with a number of our partners to try and get Congress to change that. To date, nobody has been successful in doing that. However, we learned today that Governor Inslee, he is going to be sharing a portion of the state's 1.6 billion dollars with local governments with a population under 500,000, which equates to about 300 million dollars. Counties are going to get a minimum of a quarter of a million and cities will get a minimum of 25,000 dollars. However, we got some information late this afternoon that the distribution to cities is going to be potentially based on a per capita methodology and that per capita amount will be 25 dollars. So that would equate to about 1.5 million dollars to the city of Lakewood. That would certainly help. But again, the downside to that is that the monies can only be used for new costs. It can't be used to backfill anything that we have lost to date. So we're going to be working with our state partners as well as the Treasury Department to try and figure out how we can best utilize those monies to help fill our financial gap. At the end of the day, really our hope is on another CARES Act economic stimulus package dedicated specifically for local governments here in Washington State, including our own Congressman Denny Heck. Our federal delegation strongly supports that and has been an advocate for that for a number of weeks, if not a couple of months now. We have been told on a number of occasions that the next stimulus package which they're calling 4.0, they call the last one 3.5, is going to include assistance for local governments, including the ability that those dollars would be able to backfill lost revenue. The challenge with that is it hasn't happened yet and we don't know when and if it's going to happen, which means that we need to plan that that money's not going to be here. We at least need to go be diligent in our efforts to plan accordingly. I mentioned the state money, the $300 million coming from the state. Pierce County has also received $158 million.
